params.question: A patient's blood test shows serum ferritin of 8 ng/mL, but haemoglobin, MCV, and serum iron are all normal. Which iron pool is being depleted at this stage?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The transport pool depletes in stage 2, when serum iron falls and TIBC rises. Normal serum iron here means transport iron is still intact.
The functional pool depletes last (stage 3), producing low haemoglobin and low MCV. Normal haemoglobin confirms this pool is untouched.

Correct. Ferritin directly reflects storage iron in the liver and macrophages. A low ferritin with normal haemoglobin and serum iron indicates isolated storage depletion — the earliest and most treatable stage of iron deficiency.
Iron depletion follows a strict sequence: storage → transport → functional. Simultaneous depletion would show low serum iron and low haemoglobin, neither of which is present here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Iron depletion follows a predictable sequence: the storage pool (ferritin) empties first, then the transport pool (serum iron falls, TIBC rises), and finally the functional pool (haemoglobin drops). A low ferritin with otherwise normal values pinpoints stage 1 — storage depletion.
Exactly right. Iron depletion is sequential — storage ferritin falls first, well before serum iron or haemoglobin change. This makes ferritin the earliest laboratory warning of iron deficiency.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman has serum ferritin of 10 ng/mL, serum iron of 35 µg/dL, TIBC

params.question: A 30-year-old woman has serum ferritin of 10 ng/mL, serum iron of 35 µg/dL, TIBC of 450 µg/dL, and transferrin saturation of 8%. Her haemoglobin is 12.5 g/dL and MCV is 84 fL. Which stage of iron deficiency is she in?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In stage 1, only ferritin is low. Serum iron, TIBC, and transferrin saturation are still normal. This patient's abnormal transport markers place her beyond stage 1.
Correct. Both storage (low ferritin) and transport (low serum iron, high TIBC, transferrin saturation below 15%) are compromised, but haemoglobin and MCV remain normal — the hallmark of stage 2.
Stage 3 requires low haemoglobin and low MCV with a microcytic hypochromic smear. This patient's normal haemoglobin of 12.5 and MCV of 84 rule out stage 3.

Functional iron deficiency refers to iron trapped in macrophages during chronic inflammation, with high ferritin. This patient's low ferritin indicates genuinely depleted stores, not sequestered iron.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three stages: Stage 1 = only low ferritin. Stage 2 = low ferritin PLUS low serum iron, high TIBC, and low transferrin saturation, but haemoglobin still normal. Stage 3 = all of the above PLUS low Hb and MCV. This patient has abnormal storage and transport markers but normal Hb — stage 2.
Well done. The combination of depleted storage markers AND depleted transport markers, with preserved haemoglobin, defines stage 2 — the window where treatment prevents progression to frank anaemia.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old man with no dietary restrictions presents with iron deficiency ana

params.question: A 62-year-old man with no dietary restrictions presents with iron deficiency anaemia. He has no history of gastrectomy or coeliac disease. Which investigation is the highest priority to determine the cause?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hb electrophoresis evaluates thalassaemia and haemoglobinopathies. Iron studies have already confirmed iron deficiency, so the priority is finding the cause of iron loss, not re-evaluating the type of anaemia.

TTG antibodies screen for coeliac disease (decreased absorption). While reasonable, in an elderly male without GI symptoms of malabsorption, chronic blood loss is statistically far more likely and more dangerous to miss.

Correct. In elderly men and postmenopausal women with IDA and no clear dietary or malabsorption cause, GI bleeding from occult malignancy must be excluded first. Endoscopy is mandatory before attributing the anaemia to any other cause.

Bone marrow biopsy is the gold standard for confirming absent iron stores but is rarely needed when serum iron studies already confirm deficiency. The clinical priority is identifying the bleeding source.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the four buckets: decreased intake, decreased absorption, increased loss, and increased demand. In an elderly man without dietary restrictions or malabsorption, the most likely and most dangerous cause is chronic GI blood loss. Endoscopy is mandatory to exclude malignancy.

Correct. In an elderly male with IDA and no obvious dietary or malabsorption cause, the most dangerous possibility — GI malignancy causing chronic occult blood loss — must be ruled out by endoscopy before any other workup.

interactions.label: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis has microcytic anaemia and a serum fe

params.question: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis has microcytic anaemia and a serum ferritin of 55 ng/mL. Her clinician suspects concurrent iron deficiency despite the normal ferritin. Which additional test would best resolve this diagnostic uncertainty?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Repeating ferritin is unhelpful because the inflammation driving the false elevation persists. The ferritin will remain misleadingly elevated as long as the disease is active.
Hepcidin rises in both inflammation and iron sufficiency, making it difficult to interpret in this clinical context. It is not a standard test for distinguishing IDA from ACD.

Correct. sTfR rises when erythroblasts are iron-starved and, crucially, is not affected by inflammation. A high sTfR in this setting confirms true iron deficiency masked by an inflammation-elevated ferritin.
TIBC is suppressed by inflammation (reduced transferrin synthesis), so it may be falsely low in active RA, reducing its discriminating power. sTfR is the more reliable marker in inflammatory states.

overallFeedback.feedback: The trap: ferritin is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation independently of iron stores. In active inflammatory disease, a ferritin of 55 does not reliably exclude iron deficiency. Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) is the solution — it reflects erythroblast iron demand and is not affected by the acute phase response.

Exactly. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — a 'normal' value of 55 in active inflammation may be masking depleted stores. Soluble transferrin receptor is unaffected by inflammation and rises specifically when erythroblasts lack iron, making it the key test in this scenario.

interactions.label: A patient with chronic pulmonary tuberculosis has haemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, MCV o

params.question: A patient with chronic pulmonary tuberculosis has haemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, MCV of 78 fL, serum iron of 25 µg/dL, ferritin of 310 ng/mL, and low TIBC. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IDA shows low ferritin and high TIBC, because the body builds more transferrin to scavenge scarce iron. This patient's high ferritin and low TIBC are the opposite pattern.
Beta-thalassaemia trait shows normal iron studies (normal ferritin, normal TIBC) and is identified by raised HbA2 on HPLC. The abnormal iron studies and inflammatory context point elsewhere.

Correct. Chronic TB drives IL-6 → hepcidin → ferroportin degradation, trapping iron inside macrophages. The hallmark pattern is high ferritin (stores are full), low serum iron (iron locked away), and low TIBC (inflammation suppresses transferrin synthesis). Prolonged severe inflammation explains the microcytosis.
Sideroblastic anaemia produces a dimorphic smear with very high RDW. While ferritin and serum iron are high, TIBC is typically normal and diagnosis requires ringed sideroblasts on marrow examination.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the TIBC hook analogy: think of TIBC as iron-carrying hooks the body builds. In iron deficiency, the body builds MORE hooks (high TIBC) to grab scarce iron. In chronic inflammation, hepcidin locks iron inside macrophages and the body SUPPRESSES hook production (low TIBC). High ferritin + low TIBC + chronic infection = ACD, not IDA.

Correct. The TIBC logic is the key discriminator: an iron-starved body builds more transferrin hooks (high TIBC in IDA), while an inflamed body suppresses hook production (low TIBC in ACD). High ferritin + low TIBC + chronic infection = anaemia of chronic disease.
